chapter_summary:
Project 4 is the culmination of the hardware portion of the Nand2Tetris course. You will assemble the CPU, memory, and I/O into a complete, working computer. This is the moment when all the pieces come together: the logic gates you built in Project 1, the ALU and memory you built in Project 2, and the CPU you designed in the previous chapters.

**Project 4 specification:**

Build the following chips in HDL:
1. **CPU:** The Hack CPU with A register, D register, ALU, PC, and control logic.
2. **Memory:** The memory subsystem that combines RAM16K, screen, and keyboard.
3. **Computer:** The top-level chip that connects CPU, Memory, and ROM32K.

**CPU design:**

The CPU is the most complex chip in this project. It is built from:
- A register (Register chip from Project 2)
- D register (Register chip from Project 2)
- ALU (from Project 2)
- PC (from Project 2)
- Muxes and gates (from Project 1)

The CPU interface:
```hdl
CHIP CPU {
    IN inM[16], instruction[16], reset;
    OUT outM[16], writeM, addressM[15], pc[15];
}
```

The CPU internal logic is divided into:
1. **Instruction type detection:** Check bit 15 to distinguish A-instructions from C-instructions.
2. **A register logic:** Load A with instruction value (A-instruction) or ALU output (C-instruction with A as destination).
3. **D register logic:** Load D with ALU output (C-instruction with D as destination).
4. **ALU logic:** Select inputs (A or M), set control bits, compute result.
5. **Memory write logic:** Write ALU output to M (C-instruction with M as destination).
6. **PC logic:** Increment PC or load with A (for jumps) or reset to 0.

**Memory design:**

The Memory chip combines three address ranges:
- **RAM:** Addresses 0 to 16383 (16K words). Uses the RAM16K chip.
- **Screen:** Addresses 16384 to 24575 (8K words). Uses a memory-mapped screen device.
- **Keyboard:** Address 24576. Uses a memory-mapped keyboard device.

The Memory chip routes access based on the address:
```hdl
CHIP Memory {
    IN in[16], load, address[15];
    OUT out[16];

    PARTS:
    // Route to RAM, screen, or keyboard based on address
    // If address < 16384: access RAM16K
    // If 16384 <= address < 24576: access screen
    // If address = 24576: access keyboard
}
```

The routing is done using a DMux to select the load signal and a Mux to select the output.

**Computer design:**

The Computer chip is the top-level chip that connects everything:
```hdl
CHIP Computer {
    IN reset;

    PARTS:
    ROM32K(address=pc, out=instruction);
    CPU(inM=inM, instruction=instruction, reset=reset, outM=outM, writeM=writeM, addressM=addressM, pc=pc);
    Memory(in=outM, load=writeM, address=addressM, out=inM);
}
```

This is a complete computer! It can fetch instructions from ROM, execute them in the CPU, and read/write data from/to memory.

**Testing the computer:**

The Computer chip is tested using the Hardware Simulator with test scripts that load a program into ROM and verify the computer's behavior. The test scripts include:
- A simple program that adds two numbers.
- A program that uses conditional jumps.
- A program that writes to the screen.
- A program that reads from the keyboard.

**Running your own programs:**

Once the Computer chip is built, you can write your own assembly programs and run them on the computer using the CPU Emulator or the Hardware Simulator. The CPU Emulator is a software simulator that runs the Hack machine language without requiring the HDL implementation. It is useful for testing programs before running them on the hardware simulator.

**Writing assembly programs:**

The Hack assembly language is a symbolic version of the machine language. It uses mnemonics for instructions and allows labels and symbolic variables. For example:
```asm
// Add 2 + 3
@2
D=A
@3
D=D+A
@0
M=D

// Loop forever
(END)
@END
0;JMP
```

The assembly language is translated to machine code by the assembler (which we will build in Module 4).

screens.title: Project 4 — Building the Hack Computer
screens.subtitle: Assemble CPU, Memory, and Computer into a working Hack machine

narration.text: This chapter marks the hardware culmination of the course: you will assemble the C P U, the memory subsystem, and the top-level Computer chip to create a working Hack computer. You will bring together parts built earlier — registers, the ALU, muxes and R A M — and connect them so the machine can fetch instructions, execute them, read and write memory, and run programs. We will walk through the C P U interface and internal logic, the memory address routing that makes R A M, screen and keyboard work together, and how the Computer chip composes ROM, C P U and Memory so the fetch-execute cycle completes. You will also learn practical test and debug steps: how test scripts verify functionality, how the C P U Emulator differs from the Hardware Simulator, and how to run simple assembly programs like an add routine or the Fill screen program. By the end you should be able to explain why the C P U is the most intricate chip, why memory-mapped input and output matters, and how a bug in a single connection can stop the whole machine. Think about which part you expect to be most error-prone as you build — that reflection helps focus debugging when you start wiring the chips.

keyIdea.title: Why Project 4 matters
keyIdea.text: It unites gates, registers, ALU, RAM and I/O into a full computer you can program and test, demonstrating how low-level components implement stored-program execution.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.subtitle: What you'll be able to do after completing Project 4

narration.text: By the end of Project 4 you will have built three HDL chips and proven they work together. First, you will complete the C P U implementation including A and D registers, ALU input selection, control signals, and the program counter so the chip executes both A-instructions and C-instructions. Second, you will create the Memory chip that routes addresses to RAM16K, the memory-mapped screen device, and the keyboard address. Third, you will assemble the top-level Computer chip that ties ROM32K, the C P U and Memory together so a stored program can run. Each objective maps to concrete skills: writing HDL parts, composing mux and dmux routing, and running simulator test scripts. You will also write and run small assembly programs — an adder, a multiply-by-add loop, and an interactive Fill program — to validate your hardware. Finally, you will practice debugging by tracing the fetch-execute cycle when behavior diverges from the expected output. These objectives focus on construction, testing, and debugging, which are the core engineering tasks for building a working computer from simple components.

keyIdea.text: Implement CPU, Memory and Computer chips; run test scripts and simple assembly programs to validate system-level behavior.

screens.title: Skills You Will Practice
screens.subtitle: Testing, assembly, and debugging the complete system

narration.text: Beyond implementation, Project 4 is about verification and iteration. You will write and run test scripts in the Hardware Simulator to check ROM fetches, C P U state, memory reads and writes, and screen updates. You will practice translating simple algorithms into Hack assembly and loading them into ROM. For debugging, you will trace the fetch-execute cycle: observe the instruction fetched from ROM, watch how the C P U decodes it (A vs C instruction), inspect register values and ALU outputs, and check whether writeM and addressM drive Memory correctly. You will also compare the C P U Emulator to the HDL implementation: the emulator runs machine code directly and is a quick way to validate program logic before testing a hardware build. These skills — test-driven design, trace debugging, and program-to-hardware mapping — are the essential engineering practices for making the whole computer work. As you practice, focus on small programs that exercise one feature at a time so you can isolate and fix errors quickly.

keyIdea.title: Skill focus
keyIdea.text: Verification and debugging are as important as correct HDL wiring — use test scripts and small programs to isolate issues efficiently.

screens.title: The Computer Chip — top-level composition
screens.subtitle: Connect ROM, CPU and Memory to complete the fetch-execute cycle

narration.text: The Computer chip is the top-level HDL composition that brings ROM32K, the C P U, and Memory together into a single, working unit. Its role is simple but essential: ROM supplies the next instruction using the program counter, the C P U executes that instruction and produces a memory address, write flag and data, and Memory responds by returning the data at that address or writing to it. The provided Computer specification shows exactly how these parts are wired: ROM32K(address=pc, out=instruction); C P U(inM=inM, instruction=instruction, reset=reset, outM=outM, writeM=writeM, addressM=addressM, pc=pc); Memory(in=outM, load=writeM, address=addressM, out=inM). This composition enforces the classic fetch-decode-execute loop entirely in hardware wiring. A common misconception is that the Computer chip contains control logic; it does not — the intelligence is inside the C P U. The Computer simply connects signals so each clock step fetches an instruction and the C P U and Memory exchange data. When you test it, load a small program into ROM (for example, an add routine) and step through the simulator to observe the PC incrementing, instructions being fetched, and memory reads and writes happening. A useful check is to watch that when writeM is asserted the Memory updates the right address and outM value, because a single miswired signal there often causes visible program errors. How will you verify the wiring between C P U and Memory in your first test?

keyIdea.title: Computer is composition
keyIdea.text: The Computer chip wires ROM, CPU and Memory so the machine can fetch an instruction, execute it, and access memory; it delegates behavior to the CPU and Memory chips.

content.html:
Core Concept Computer Chip
Computer: ROM + CPU + Memory
Top-level wiring creates a working stored-program machine.
Specification (HDL)
CHIP Computer {
  IN reset;

  PARTS:
  ROM32K(address=pc, out=instruction);
  CPU(inM=inM, instruction=instruction, reset=reset,
      outM=outM, writeM=writeM, addressM=addressM, pc=pc);
  Memory(in=outM, load=writeM, address=addressM, out=inM);
}
This HDL snippet shows the exact signal names used to connect the three chips.
Checks to run
  • Load a simple add program into ROM and step through a few cycles.
  • Verify pc advances unless a jump occurs; check instruction matches ROM output.
  • When writeM is 1, confirm Memory stores outM at addressM.
Key takeaway: composition + signal naming accuracy yields a functioning system.

screens.title: CPU Interface and Responsibilities
screens.subtitle: Signals that drive memory and the program counter

narration.text: The C P U exposes a small but powerful interface that connects it to memory and to ROM. Its inputs are inM (the value read from Memory), instruction (the current 16-bit instruction from ROM), and reset. Its outputs are outM (data to write into Memory), writeM (whether to write), addressM (the memory address), and pc (the program counter value sent to ROM). These signals implement the machine-level contract: the C P U fetches an instruction, computes what address to read or write, decides whether to write, and sets the next pc value. Internally, the C P U decodes the instruction: if bit 15 is zero it's an A-instruction and the A register loads the immediate value; if bit 15 is one it's a C-instruction and the ALU performs computation controlled by instruction bits. The C P U is responsible for selecting ALU inputs (A register or Memory M), routing ALU outputs to registers or memory, and choosing how the PC updates — increment, load from A for a jump, or reset. A common misconception is that the C P U alone knows memory contents; it does not — it only reads inM and writes outM. When debugging, inspect the addressM and writeM lines to confirm the C P U intends the correct memory operation at the right moment.

keyIdea.title: CPU contract
keyIdea.text: The CPU translates instructions into control signals and data flow: outM, writeM and addressM implement memory operations; pc steers ROM fetches.

content.html:
Architecture CPU Interface
CPU Inputs & Outputs
Formal interface
<!-- Representation for clarity -->
CHIP CPU {
  IN inM[16], instruction[16], reset;
  OUT outM[16], writeM, addressM[15], pc[15];
}
inM and outM carry 16-bit data; addressM chooses which memory word the CPU accesses.
Why each signal matters
  • writeM: when high, causes Memory to store outM at addressM; check this to validate writes.
  • pc: selects the next ROM address; control logic chooses increment, load, or reset.
  • inM: the only way the CPU reads memory contents; stale inM yields incorrect ALU inputs.
Common-mistake
Confusing addressM bit-width or miswiring writeM can silently prevent writes without other visible errors. Always observe these signals in early tests.

screens.title: CPU Internal Logic: Instruction Types and Registers
screens.subtitle: How A-instructions and C-instructions drive register behavior

narration.text: Inside the C P U the first step is instruction type detection: check bit 15. If bit 15 is zero, the instruction is an A-instruction and its remaining 15 bits are an immediate value to load into the A register. If bit 15 is one, it's a C-instruction containing ALU control bits, destination bits and jump bits. The A register has two load pathways: load from the immediate value for A-instructions, or load from the ALU output when a C-instruction targets A. The D register loads from ALU output when the C-instruction's destination includes D. This split of responsibilities is important: A holds addresses or constants, D holds temporary computations, and the A register also serves as an ALU input or a source for PC loads during jumps. Concretely, a mistake learners often make is wiring the A register only to accept immediate loads; it must also accept ALU output under the correct destination control. To test this, run an instruction that sets A from an immediate and then a subsequent C-instruction that writes to A, and observe the A register contents change accordingly. The takeaway is that correct multiplexing and load control at each register is central to C P U correctness.

keyIdea.title: Registers and instruction types
keyIdea.text: Bit 15 selects A vs C instructions; registers have conditional load paths from immediate values or ALU output depending on instruction decode.

content.html:
Process Flow Instruction Types & Registers
A vs C Instructions and Register Loads
Instruction type detection
  • If bit 15 = 0 → A-instruction: A ← instruction[0..14].
  • If bit 15 = 1 → C-instruction: decode ALU controls, destinations, jumps.
Test: fetch an A-instruction and check A's new value equals the immediate.
Register load logic
  • A register: loads immediate (A-instruction) or ALU output (C-instruction with A as destination).
  • D register: loads ALU output when C-instruction destination includes D.
  • PC: increment, load A for jump, or reset to zero.
Common mistake: not multiplexing ALU vs immediate for A-register loads.
Example
Run sequence: @5 (A←5), D=A, @10 (A←10), A=D. Watch A change both from immediate and from ALU result when destination bits target A.

screens.title: ALU and Input Selection
screens.subtitle: Choosing A or M as the second ALU operand

narration.text: The ALU computes arithmetic and logical operations based on control bits encoded in C-instructions. A key implementation detail is how the second ALU input is selected: the C P U must choose between the A register and the memory value M (the content of R A M at addressM). This selection uses a mux controlled by a single instruction bit. If the instruction specifies M as the ALU input, the C P U supplies inM to the ALU; otherwise it supplies A. The ALU's result can then be routed to the D register, to the A register, or to outM for writing to Memory, depending on the destination bits. A frequent misconception is assuming that ALU input selection only affects arithmetic; in practice it also controls whether the C P U reads from memory or uses an immediate/address stored in A, which affects both computation and address generation. When you test ALU behavior, include programs that compute D=D+M and D=D+A to verify the mux selection is correct. Also watch the ALU control bits to ensure the expected operation (e. g., addition vs logical AND) occurs. The takeaway: correct input selection into the ALU is essential to implement both memory-dependent operations and register-only computations.

keyIdea.title: ALU input mux
keyIdea.text: A single mux decides whether the ALU receives A or M; this choice enables computations that use memory values or register values interchangeably.

content.html:
Core Concept ALU Input Selection
Selecting A or M for the ALU
Mux control
A C-instruction bit selects ALU input: when set, use M (inM); otherwise use A register. This implements memory-based operations.
Test sequences: D=D+M and D=D+A should produce different results if RAM[addr] differs from A.
Routing ALU output
  • Destination bits decide whether ALU output goes to A, D, M (outM) or any combination.
  • When outM is written, Memory must update addressM with the correct address for the write.
Common mistake: forgetting to connect ALU output to outM when M is a destination, causing writes to be stale or zero.

screens.title: Memory Chip: Address-based Routing
screens.subtitle: Routing requests between RAM, screen, and keyboard

narration.text: The Memory chip combines three address ranges into a single interface: RAM16K for addresses 0..16383, the screen mapped to 16384..24575, and the keyboard at address 24576. The Memory chip receives in[16] data to write, a load signal, and a 15-bit address. Internally it uses a demultiplexer on the load signal to enable only the selected device to write, and a multiplexer on the outputs to return the active device's data on out. Concretely: if address < 16384, route to RAM16K; if 16384 <= address < 24576, route to the screen device; if address == 24576, read-only keyboard device. A practical detail is ensuring address comparisons are correct and that the load enable reaches only the chosen R A M or screen component. A common mistake is miscalculating the address boundaries or using the wrong bit width, which can cause reads from the wrong device or accidental writes to screen memory. To validate, run memory tests that write to low addresses and to screen addresses and ensure the expected words change. Also test reading keyboard address for correct read-only behavior. Memory-mapped input and output is powerful: it allows the C P U to treat peripherals as ordinary memory locations, but correct routing is critical for safe operation.

keyIdea.title: Memory mapping
keyIdea.text: Memory presents RAM, screen and keyboard under one address space; dmux and mux logic route loads and outputs based on the address range.

content.html:
Definition Memory mapping
Memory: RAM16K, Screen, Keyboard
Address ranges
  • 0..16383 → RAM16K
  • 16384..24575 → Screen (8K)
  • 24576 → Keyboard (single address)
Use dmux to route load and mux to select out depending on address.
Testing tips
Write unique values to sample RAM and screen addresses, then read them back. Confirm keyboard address reads reflect simulated key state and is not writable.
Common mistake: off-by-one address checks or wrong bit-width in address decoding.

screens.title: Testing the Computer: Test Scripts and Examples
screens.subtitle: Use the Hardware Simulator with provided scripts

narration.text: Testing the Computer chip uses the Hardware Simulator and the provided test scripts that load programs into ROM and step the machine. Typical tests included with the project exercise arithmetic, conditional jumps, screen writes, and keyboard reads. For example, a simple add test places constants or values in ROM that compute the sum of two numbers and check that the result is written to the expected R A M address. Another script runs a conditional-jump program to verify that the PC loads correctly when a jump condition is satisfied. Screen tests write pixel words to screen memory and confirm that the memory-mapped screen words were updated. The test scripts make it possible to spot where behavior diverges: if the add test fails, inspect ALU outputs and whether writeM/addressM signals align with expected cycles. A common debugging pattern is to test one subsystem at a time: validate the C P U with the emulator on machine code, validate Memory routing independently, then combine them in the Computer chip. Running small, focused tests shortens the debug loop and helps you isolate wiring errors efficiently. Which small test will you run first to build confidence in your wiring?

keyIdea.title: Test strategy
keyIdea.text: Run targeted test scripts for arithmetic, jumps and I/O to validate each subsystem before full integration; isolate failures by checking control signals.

content.html:
Process Flow Testing the Computer
Using the Hardware Simulator
Typical test scripts
  • Add two numbers and verify RAM[2] contains the sum.
  • Conditional jumps: verify PC changes when a jump condition is true.
  • Screen writes: check that screen memory words are written.
Debugging steps
  1. Run emulator on the machine code to confirm program logic.
  2. Run hardware test script and trace the instruction and signals.
  3. Inspect writeM, addressM and outM for failed writes.

screens.title: CPU Emulator vs Hardware Simulator
screens.subtitle: When to use the emulator and when to test the HDL implementation

narration.text: Two simulators help you validate programs and hardware: the C P U Emulator and the Hardware Simulator. The C P U Emulator executes Hack machine code directly in software. Use it to check program logic quickly without building HDL — it tells you whether your assembly turns into the correct sequence of operations. The Hardware Simulator runs the actual HDL chips you built; it verifies that your wiring reproduces the expected machine behavior. Both have complementary strengths: use the emulator to validate algorithms and to step through instruction-level behavior rapidly, then use the hardware simulator to find wiring mistakes in registers, muxes, or control signals. A common misconception is that passing the emulator guarantees the HDL will work; it does not, because HDL errors like a miswired dmux or an inverted load signal can break the hardware even when the machine code is correct. A good workflow is: validate the program in the emulator, assemble machine code, then load into ROM and run the hardware test scripts. When a mismatch appears, trace specific signals — instruction, pc, writeM, addressM and inM — to locate the faulty connection. Which part would you inspect first when emulator and hardware results diverge?

keyIdea.title: Complementary tools
keyIdea.text: Use the emulator for fast program checks and the hardware simulator to validate HDL wiring; passing one does not guarantee the other.

content.html:
Comparison Emulator vs Hardware
Emulator and Hardware Simulator
CPU Emulator
Runs machine code directly; fast validation for program logic; no HDL required.
Use it first to check algorithms and jump logic.
Hardware Simulator
Executes your HDL chips; validates wiring, mux/dmux behavior and register load logic.
Use it to find wiring errors after emulator tests pass.

screens.title: Writing Assembly: Add and Loop Examples
screens.subtitle: Concrete assembly snippets and what they do in hardware

narration.text: Writing assembly for the Hack computer is the bridge between algorithms and machine behavior. A simple example that adds two numbers and stores the result in R A M[0] follows the pattern: load a constant or read a R A M address into a register, perform ALU operations, and write back. For example the classic add snippet uses @2, D=A, @3, D=D+A, @0, M=D to place 2+3 into R A M[0]. The assembler will translate these symbols into the corresponding machine codes. The code runs in the C P U by fetching each instruction from ROM, updating registers and the ALU, and performing writes to memory when writeM is asserted. Another pattern is an infinite loop: define a label (END), then @END, 0;JMP to jump unconditionally by loading the A register with the label address and setting the jump bits. When you run these programs on hardware, watch the pc values, register contents and memory writes: the add program should show D receiving intermediate results and M updating at the target address. A misconception students have is thinking labels are hardware constructs — labels are assembly conveniences resolved by the assembler; the hardware only sees numeric addresses. After running the add example, try writing a slightly larger program and use the emulator first, then the hardware test scripts to confirm behavior.

keyIdea.title: Assembly to machine
keyIdea.text: Assembly mnemonics map to machine instructions; run examples in the emulator first, then test on hardware to confirm register and memory effects.

content.html:
Example Assembly snippets
Add 2 + 3 and Loop forever
Add program (assembly)
// Add 2 + 3
@2
D=A
@3
D=D+A
@0
M=D

// Loop forever
(END)
@END
0;JMP
Run this first in the emulator; then load into ROM and step through the hardware simulator to watch memory update.
What to observe
  • After D=D+A, D holds the sum; after @0 followed by M=D, RAM[0] stores the result.
  • After jump to END, pc holds the label address and remains there in the infinite loop.

screens.title: Hands-On Programs: Multiply and Fill
screens.subtitle: Implement multiply-by-add and the Fill screen program

narration.text: The hands-on activity asks you to write three programs: add two numbers, multiply via repeated addition, and the Fill screen program that responds to keyboard state. For multiplication, the approach is algorithmic: read multiplicand and multiplier from R A M, initialize an accumulator to zero, and loop adding the multiplicand while decrementing the multiplier until it reaches zero. This demonstrates how control flow maps to jumps and register operations. The Fill screen program demonstrates memory-mapped input and output: it reads the keyboard address (24576); if non-zero, it writes the value 0xFFFF to every screen word (addresses 16384..24575), otherwise writes 0x0000. At the hardware level, each write asserts writeM and sets addressM to the current screen address while outM contains the pixel word. The program runs in an infinite loop so it continuously monitors keyboard state. Debugging these programs on hardware requires you to watch repeated writes to screen addresses and ensure the keyboard read remains read-only. When implementing multiply, test with small non-negative numbers to verify repeated addition correctly accumulates. For Fill, test by simulating a key press in the hardware simulator and observing screen memory change. These tasks reinforce the connection between assembly control flow and memory operations in hardware.

keyIdea.title: Practice programs
keyIdea.text: Small programs such as repeated addition and Fill exercise loops, memory writes, and memory-mapped I/O, tying software logic to hardware signals.

content.html:
Hands-on Activity Multiply & Fill
Multiply by repeated addition; Fill screen on key
Multiply outline
  1. Load RAM[0] multiplicand into D.
  2. Load RAM[1] multiplier into A or temp register.
  3. Loop: add multiplicand to accumulator, decrement multiplier, jump until zero.
  4. Store result into RAM[2].
Fill program behavior
Continuously read keyboard (address 24576). If non-zero, write 0xFFFF to addresses 16384..24575; otherwise write 0x0000. Runs in an infinite loop.
Debug tip
Simulate a key press and step through the program to see repeated writes to the screen addresses; watch writeM and addressM change as the loop iterates.

screens.title: PC Logic: Increment, Load, Reset
screens.subtitle: How the CPU chooses the next instruction address

narration.text: The program counter (PC) inside the C P U controls which ROM address is fetched next. The PC logic implements three behaviors: increment (advance to the next instruction), load (set the PC to the A register, typically for jumps), and reset (set PC to zero). The C-instruction's jump bits determine whether the ALU output indicates that a jump should occur; if the condition holds, the PC loads with A. Otherwise, the default behavior is to increment. Reset forces PC back to zero regardless of other signals. Implementing this requires both conditional logic based on ALU zero/negative flags and correct load control for the PC register. A misconception is thinking jump changes the ALU operation only; in fact a jump commonly depends on an ALU result and then changes pc by loading A. When testing, create a small program that sets up a conditional jump (for example, decrementing a counter and jumping while non-zero) and observe pc either incrementing or loading A. Also test the reset behavior explicitly by asserting reset and confirming pc becomes zero. Correct PC behavior is essential for control flow and conditional looping to function as expected in your programs.

keyIdea.title: PC control
keyIdea.text: PC updates by increment, by loading A on a jump, or by reset; jump decisions depend on ALU flags evaluated by the CPU control logic.

content.html:
Core Concept Program Counter (PC)
PC: increment, load A, or reset
Update rules
  • Default: pc ← pc + 1
  • If jump condition true: pc ← A
  • If reset signal asserted: pc ← 0
Test & debug
Validate jumps by setting up a counter and looping with conditionals. Use reset tests to ensure the system can restart predictably.

screens.title: Why the CPU is the Hardest Chip to Build
screens.subtitle: Complex internal logic, many interconnections and error-prone wiring

narration.text: Of the three chips in Project 4 — C P U, Memory and Computer — the C P U is the most complex and the most error-prone. It contains multiple registers with conditional load logic, the ALU and its input-selection muxes, the PC with conditional update rules, and the instruction decode logic that translates bits into control signals. Unlike Memory, which is mainly routing and address-based selection, the C P U must implement many internal decision points and coordinate the timing of loads, ALU operations and writes. Small wiring mistakes, such as an inverted load control or a misplaced mux input, can cause subtle failures that break entire programs. Yet the C P U is also the most interesting: it is where the machine’s behavior is specified and where choices about register usage, ALU control, and jump decisions are realized. When you build the C P U, approach it modularly: test registers and ALU components independently, then integrate and test instruction decoding, and finally validate PC and memory interactions together. This staged integration reduces the search space when bugs appear and helps you focus on fixing the single wrong connection that often causes the biggest problems.

keyIdea.title: CPU complexity
keyIdea.text: The CPU has the densest internal logic and the most control signals; modular testing reduces debugging time and surface area for errors.

Reflection Why CPU is hardest
CPU: most internal logic and interconnections
Many components
Registers, ALU, muxes, PC and control decode increase wiring complexity.
Error-prone signals

Integration strategy
Test parts independently, then integrate instruction decode and PC logic last.

narration.text: Project 4 brings each previously built component into a single functioning computer. Remember three central facts: first, the Computer chip composes ROM, C P U and Memory so the fetch-execute loop completes; the Computer itself contains no control logic beyond wiring. Second, the C P U is the locus of complexity: it decodes instructions, controls register loads, selects ALU inputs, and updates the PC, producing writeM, addressM and outM signals that drive memory. Third, the Memory chip uses address-based routing to combine RAM16K, a memory-mapped screen, and the keyboard. Testing strategy matters: validate programs in the C P U Emulator, run targeted hardware test scripts, and inspect signals like pc, writeM and addressM to find wiring errors. Practically, small programs — add, repeated addition for multiply, and Fill for memory-mapped input and output — exercise core behaviors. As you test and debug, modularize your work and focus on one subsystem at a time. Which of these key concepts will you use first as you begin wiring your chips?

keyIdea.title: Remember
keyIdea.text: Composition, CPU control complexity, and memory mapping are the essential lessons — test each piece independently then integrate.

content.html:
Key Concepts What to Remember
System Composition
ROM + CPU + Memory wired together create the stored-program computer.
CPU Complexity
Instruction decode, register loads, ALU selection and PC logic must be correct.
Memory Mapping
Use address ranges to route loads and outputs to RAM, screen, or keyboard.
Key Takeaway

Approach Project 4 modularly: test the CPU, verify memory routing, then integrate into the Computer. Focus on the signals pc, addressM and writeM when debugging.

screens.title: What to Remember
screens.subtitle: Short concept cards to carry forward

narration.text: Before you start the build, keep three concise reminders in mind. First, test often: use the emulator for program logic and the hardware simulator for HDL wiring. Second, isolate components: validate registers, ALU, and RAM16K separately before full integration to reduce debugging complexity. Third, remember memory-mapped input and output: treating screen and keyboard as memory locations simplifies programs but requires careful address routing. These three practices will make the engineering process manageable and help you find single-point wiring errors quickly. As you begin wiring the C P U, decide which small test you will run first — that plan keeps debugging focused and efficient. What to Remember means test early, modularize your build, and treat peripherals as memory; plan a first test to validate a critical signal path.. In practical terms, short concept cards to carry forward. A simple real-world example is helpful here, because students learn best when they can connect the idea to a familiar situation. This matters because it gives the learner a clear mental model and helps them connect the concept to later examples and problems. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Practical reminders
keyIdea.text: Test early, modularize your build, and treat peripherals as memory; plan a first test to validate a critical signal path.

content.html:
What to Remember Quick reference
Test early
Emulator then hardware simulator to separate program errors from wiring errors.
Build modularly
Validate registers, ALU and RAM independently to narrow bugs.
Memory I/O
Screen and keyboard are memory addresses; ensure correct address decoding to use them safely.
Final takeaway

Approach Project 4 as an engineering integration: plan small tests, validate components, and iterate until the whole machine runs your programs.
